$comment: TYPOGRAPHY — ONE SWITCH.  Change a value in `active` and every logo wordmark, document, slide and social card follows on the next `npm run build`. Nothing downstream names a font; templates ask for role `arabic.wordmark` or `latin.content` and this file decides what that is. Switch from the CLI with `npm run font:set arabic.content=noto-naskh-arabic`, which validates the choice against the catalogue and rebuilds.  RULE: two Arabic faces, never three. One draws wordmarks, one sets content. A wordmark face is picked for a handful of letters at one size; a content face is picked for paragraphs. Keeping them apart is what stops a document from slowly starting to look like a logo. The Latin side mirrors the split for French.

active.$description: THE SWITCH. Each value is EITHER a key in `catalog` whose `roles` allow that use, OR the name of another role on the same script, which makes it an alias. `npm run check:fonts` fails the build otherwise.
active.$roles: wordmark = logo lockups. content = documents, slides, cards. motto = the motto on the roundel-motto lockup, which is set on a curve at about a third the wordmark's size and can reasonably want a face of its own.
active.$aliases: `"motto": "content"` means the motto follows whatever the content face is. That is the default, and it is what keeps the count at two faces per script. Point it at a catalogue key instead and the motto gets its own face — a deliberate third, not an accident.

motto.$description: How the motto is set, beyond which face draws it. Its geometry — radius, size and sweep on the roundel — is `logo.motto` in space.json.
motto.$weight: The motto runs small and on a curve, where a regular weight goes thin. Ignored by a face that has no weight above its default.

catalog.$description: Vetted faces. Every one is SIL Open Font Licence, so the association can embed it in a PDF and hand files to a print shop without asking permission. `roles` says what a face may be switched in as; `scripts` says what it can actually set. To add a face: put the files in brand/fonts/<key>/ with its OFL.txt, add an entry here, then switch to it.

tajawal.$note: The wordmark face for BOTH scripts. Its Latin is drawn to sit with its Arabic, so the French and Arabic marks are the same family rather than a pairing that has to be judged — and it matches the letterforms already in the existing mark. Set Latin at 800 to hold its weight beside the Arabic.

reem-kufi.$note: The strongest alternative wordmark. Geometric kufi, built for display; more distinctive than Tajawal but less warm. Never use for content — it has no comfortable reading weight.

ibm-plex-sans-arabic.$note: The choice if AJVT ever needs a screen-first content face — it holds up far better than Amiri at 12px.

amiri.$note: Current content face. The naskh already used in the association's décisions, règlements and official seal — it is what an AJVT paper looks like.

noto-naskh-arabic.$note: Safest fallback. Plainer than Amiri, wider language coverage, and renders identically on every device — worth switching to if printed documents ever come back wrong from a print shop.

inter.$note: A neutral grotesque. Correct but anonymous next to a heavy geometric Arabic, which is why the Latin wordmark moved to Tajawal. Still the right choice for a UI or a dense table.

outfit.$note: Geometric with near-circular bowls. AVOID for wordmarks containing a double t: it joins the crossbars, and "Taguilalett" ends up reading as "TaguilaleH".

poppins.$note: Geometric with a tall x-height, warm and round. The best option if the French should be visibly its own face rather than Tajawal's Latin. Set it a weight lighter or it overpowers the Arabic.

montserrat.$note: Wide and sturdy. Reads well small, but its width makes a long name like Taguilalett dominate a horizontal lockup.

eb-garamond.$note: Current Latin content face. The serif already used in the Termes de référence; pairs with Amiri at a similar optical weight, which is what lets a bilingual page hold together.

source-serif-4.$note: Switch here if EB Garamond reads too light next to a heavier Arabic content face.

pairing.$description: Optical correction, applied by the theme. Arabic and Latin faces almost never share an x-height, so a bilingual line looks mismatched unless one side is nudged. This is the nudge, per active pair. Regenerate with `npm run font:calibrate` after switching.
pairing.$note: Amiri sets smaller than EB Garamond at the same pt. 1.08 makes them read as equals on a bilingual cover page.

scale.$description: A 1.25 major-third scale on a 16px base. Documents, slides and cards all step through this, which is why a heading in a PDF and a heading on a card feel related.

leading.$note: Naskh needs more leading than a Latin serif — the dots below the line collide with the next line's ascenders at 1.6. Never set an Arabic paragraph tighter than 1.8; the document theme enforces it.
